title: Ogham
otherNames: Old Irish ogam, Modern Irish ogham
the feda (letters; singular fid, "wood, tree, letter")
family: Insular epigraphic alphabet of stroke-letters cut along a stemline. It was devised for Primitive Irish, almost certainly by someone who knew the Latin alphabet and Latin grammatical teaching. It is not derived from Hebrew, and it is not one of Agrippa's alphabets. The later medieval tradition elaborated it into a learned and cryptic ("secret") art.
summary: Ogham writes twenty letters (feda) as groups of one to five strokes set against a stemline. In four groups (aicmi) of five, the strokes fall on one side, on the other, across the line, or as notches on it; the manuscript tradition later added five supplementary letters (forfeda). It is first found on roughly 400 stone inscriptions around the Irish Sea, most of them in southern Ireland and most dated to the 5th-6th centuries; the script itself probably goes back to the 4th century. Its key and its lore come from much later manuscripts, whose earliest copies are late 14th-century: the Auraicept na nÉces and In Lebor Ogaim (the "Ogam Tract"), which lists many cryptic "oghams". The doctrine that every letter is a tree is medieval scholarship; the tree calendar is Robert Graves's (The White Goddess, 1948).

firstAttestation.work: Orthodox ogham inscriptions on standing stones (corpus: Macalister, CIIC I, 1945; Ziegler 1994; McManus 1991; DIAS 'Ogham in 3D' and its successor OG(H)AM project)
firstAttestation.author: anonymous
firstAttestation.date: Most orthodox inscriptions are dated to the 5th and 6th centuries AD (Wikipedia, 'Ogham inscription'). The script itself is probably older: the OG(H)AM project dates its origin 'probably' to the 4th century, and Wikipedia notes that some letters were no longer spoken by the 5th century, which implies earlier writing on perishable material. No stone carries a date; dating is by language (Primitive Irish), formulae and comparison with the Latin-inscribed stones of Britain.
firstAttestation.place: Around the Irish Sea: most Irish stones are in Munster (Co. Kerry and Cork above all); outside Ireland most are in Wales, chiefly the south-west (old Dyfed; Pembrokeshire has the most); others in Scotland, the Isle of Man and England near the Devon/Cornwall border (Wikipedia, 'Ogham inscription'; BabelStone). The outlier at Silchester (Hampshire) is from memory [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked].
firstAttestation.locator: No single locator: it is a corpus. CIIC numbers (Macalister 1945, 1949); DIAS 'Ogham in 3D' / OG(H)AM entries (https://ogham.celt.dias.ie/menu.php?lang=en).
firstAttestation.notes: Counts differ by source and by what is counted. About 400 surviving orthodox stone inscriptions (Wikipedia, 'Ogham inscription'). Ziegler (1994) is reported (Wikipedia) to list 344 Gaelic inscriptions known to Macalister in Ireland and the Isle of Man, plus seven found later. Wales: 'more than 40' in one source in the search results, but 35 stones with definite ogham in the BabelStone blog (2010); give both. Scotland: about 34 on stone plus 5 on portable objects (BabelStone blog, 2013), many in Pictish areas and some in Pictish rather than Gaelic. The OG(H)AM project counts c. 640 examples of ogham writing in all media, origin to the mid-19th century (Maynooth University project page). Typical formula: X MAQI Y, '(the stone) of X son of Y', names in the genitive; other formula words (MUCOI, AVI, ANM, KOI, CELI) are from memory [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked]. The KEY to names and values is attested much later, in manuscripts. The Auraicept na nÉces: Wikipedia ('Auraicept na n-Éces') says its core may date to the early 8th century, with much added later, and that the earliest copies are late 14th-century; tradition ascribes the first book to Cenn Fáelad (d. 679). The researcher's 'Ahlqvist (1983) dates the core to the 7th century' was not found in any source and has been removed; Ahlqvist's own dating was not checked. In Lebor Ogaim survives in the Book of Ballymote (RIA MS 23 P 12) and later manuscripts; the shelfmark and the date c. 1390 are from memory [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked].

transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Pairs ogham with Latin capitals. Castell Dwyran (Carmarthenshire), found near the church in 1895, carries a cross, a Latin inscription naming VOTEPORIGIS and an ogham one reading VOTECORIGAS (Wikipedia 'Vortiporius'; Carmarthenshire Museums' 'Selected treasure: Vortipor' page). The Latin is read as 'the memorial of Voteporix the Protector'; the exact wording MEMORIA VOTEPORIGIS PROTICTORIS is from memory [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked]. Rhŷs identified him with Gildas's Vortiporius; Patrick Sims-Williams rejected the identification on linguistic grounds (the ogham lacks the r), and Nancy Edwards (2007) suggested an earlier family member (as reported by Wikipedia and earlybritishkingdoms.com). The bilinguals later confirmed the values of the manuscript key.

claims.claim: Ogma mac Elathan invented ogham, devising it for the learned apart from rustics and herdsmen.
claims.evidence: Origin story told in In Lebor Ogaim / the Auraicept tradition. It is a medieval learned myth, reported as such.

claims.claim: The first thing written in ogham was seven b's on a birch rod, a warning to Lug mac Ethlenn; that is why b stands first.
claims.evidence: Same tract. An aetiological tale for the letter order [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked].

claims.claim: The letter names were taken from the names of the 25 best scholars in the school of Fénius Farsaid (after Babel), or from trees.
claims.evidence: Auraicept na nÉces gives both explanations, inside its account of Fénius forming Irish from the languages of Babel.

claims.claim: Every ogham letter is named after a tree.
claims.evidence: The medieval tracts assign a tree to every letter. That is documented as medieval doctrine. But several names are ordinary words: úath "fear", tinne "ingot", gort "field", straif "sulphur", úr "earth". McManus shows the Bríatharogam kennings often point to these non-tree senses (e.g. kennings of tinne about weapons and metal). Only beithe, fern, sail, dair and coll are secure tree names, with ailm and onn possible.

claims.claim: Ogham was devised by about the 4th century AD (perhaps earlier) by someone schooled in Latin grammar.
claims.evidence: Majority scholarly view on the Latin model: the split into vowels and consonant classes and the letter inventory reflect Latin grammatical analysis, and the language of the stones is Primitive Irish. Date: the OG(H)AM project gives the origin as 'probably' 4th-century; Wikipedia notes letters for sounds no longer spoken by the 5th century, implying earlier use on perishable material. Alternatives: a cipher (Carney 1975); runic inspiration (older, minority); a druidic finger code from a Greek alphabet (Macalister 1937; abandoned). The place (Ireland, or Irish settlers in Roman Britain) remains open.

claims.claim: Ogham was a secret script of the druids.
claims.evidence: The stones are public memorials with plain formulae, not secrets. "Secret" applies to the medieval learned tradition: ogham as part of the poets' and grammarians' curriculum, the saga motif of messages only the learned can read, and the cryptic varieties in In Lebor Ogaim. No source contemporary with pagan druids describes ogham.

claims.claim: The c. 100 "secret" oghams of In Lebor Ogaim were used in real communication.
claims.evidence: They are documented as lists. Most are acrostics (each letter replaced by a word from one class: birds, colours, crafts, kings, rivers...) or graphic variants. Scholars generally treat them as scholastic exercises and mnemonics. Their actual use in messages is unattested outside literature.

claims.claim: Hand ogham (cos-ogam "shin ogham", srón-ogam "nose ogham") was a working sign language.
claims.evidence: The tract describes fingers laid against the shin or the ridge of the nose as stemline. That it was practised, rather than described, is not shown.

claims.claim: Druids divined with ogham-inscribed yew rods.
claims.evidence: Tochmarc Étaíne has the druid Dalán use four yew rods inscribed with ogham to discover where Étaín is. The tale is preserved in c. 1100 and later manuscripts. It is literary evidence only.

claims.claim: Ogham stones also served as markers of land ownership.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia ('Ogham inscription') states that orthodox inscriptions record a name 'either as a cenotaph or tombstone, or documenting land ownership'. The scholarly argument (from Old Irish legal references to ogham in stone as evidence of title, and from the siting of stones) is the researcher's recollection of Charles-Edwards and Swift 1997 [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked].

claims.claim: The word "ogam" derives from the god Ogma (cf. Gaulish Ogmios in Lucian).
claims.evidence: The etymology is uncertain. Proposals include a link with Ogma/Ogmios and with Greek ógmos "furrow, line" (discussed by McManus). Lucian's Ogmios is a Gaulish Heracles figure of eloquence, and the link to the Irish Ogma is speculative.

claims.claim: The 13-month Celtic tree calendar (Birch, Rowan, Ash, Alder, Willow, Hawthorn, Oak, Holly, Hazel, Vine, Ivy, Reed, Elder) is an ancient druidic calendar.
claims.evidence: Graves presents it so in The White Goddess (1948), building on O'Flaherty's 1685 Beth-Luis-Nion order. No medieval Irish source contains a tree calendar. Historians treat it as Graves's poetic construction.

claims.claim: The Beth-Luis-Nion order (N third) is the ancient order.
claims.evidence: The Auraicept and In Lebor Ogaim have B L F S N. The stones carry texts, not alphabet rows, so they do not decide the order. N third is O'Flaherty's (1685) arrangement, followed by Graves.

claims.claim: Charles Graves, Bishop of Limerick and a 19th-century ogham scholar, was Robert Graves's grandfather.
claims.evidence: Family relationship well established in biographies of Robert Graves [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked].

claims.claim: Unicode encodes Ogham at U+1680-U+169C; U+1680 is a (visible) space character.
claims.evidence: Re-checked in the fact-check: Python unicodedata (UCD 14.0.0) gives U+1680 category Zs, U+1681-169A Lo with the names used here, U+169B Ps, U+169C Pe, U+169D-169F unassigned; Node: ' '.trim() returns '' and /\s/ matches it; Python re \s matches it.

claims.claim: Ogham is not among the alphabets of Agrippa's De occulta philosophia.
claims.evidence: Checked in the fact-check against the keyed EEBO-TCP text of the 1651 English translation (A26565, Wing A789): the words ogham/ogam/ogum, Irish, Ireland and Hibern- do not occur. Book III, chap. XXIX ('Of the Characters and Seals of spirits') gives the Theban characters 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes'; chap. XXX ('Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists') gives the Hebrew-based alphabets (Celestial, Malachim, Transitus fluvii, per the verified celestial and malachim files). The 1533 Latin was not searched, and the keyed text does not render the alphabet plates. Whether any other Renaissance grimoire prints ogham was not checked, so the claim is limited to Agrippa.
sources: Agrippa, Three Books of Occult Philosophy, trans. J. F. (London, 1651), EEBO-TCP A26565

letters.name: beithe
letters.form: One straight stroke hanging perpendicular BELOW the horizontal stemline (to the RIGHT of a vertical stemline read upward). Each stroke touches the line and stops there; none crosses it. Each stroke is about 11 stemline-thicknesses long (381 units) and about twice as thick as the line (73 vs 33 units). Glyph advance 301 units.
letters.note: Name spellings vary: Old Irish (as given), Modern Irish and the Unicode name (BEITH) differ. nameMeaning follows McManus 1988/1991 as remembered. medievalTreeGloss is the tree that the medieval tracts assign. gravesTree is the tree of The White Goddess (1948). These are three different layers; do not merge them. Fact-check: form re-measured from the Noto Sans Ogham 2.001 outlines and found exact; code point and Unicode name confirmed against UCD 14.0. NOT verified (the search budget ran out), and still the researcher's recollection: nameMeaning, medievalTreeGloss, gravesTree and the kenning. Form judgement: consistent with the standard form (strokes on one side of the stemline: B-group below / to the right, H-group above / to the left).

It is as thick as a stroke (73 units) and shorter than the line: it starts 94 units in and stops about 128 units before the line ends (x 94-495 of 623). There are no upright strokes. It looks like an equals sign whose lower bar is shorter. Glyph advance 589.
letters.note: A late scholastic sign for p, a sound the original alphabet lacked. Unicode encodes it separately from ifín/pín. The name peithboc is usually explained as 'soft b' [not verified: the fact-check search budget ran out before this was checked]. The font form is measured; its manuscript basis was not checked. Fact-check: form re-measured from the Noto Sans Ogham 2.001 outlines and found exact; code point and Unicode name confirmed against UCD 14.0. NOT verified (the search budget ran out), and still the researcher's recollection: the names and glosses. Form judgement: consistent in kind with the modern printed form as this checker knows it, but not compared with the Unicode code chart or any manuscript; medium stays. Do not caption it as a manuscript form.
letters.aicme: supplementary (not one of the five forfeda)

marks.form: A bare stretch of stemline (x 0-479, y 281-314), with no strokes.
marks.note: Unicode general category Zs, a space separator, checked in this session. It is the word divider in Ogham text, and it is drawn VISIBLY as stemline. In JavaScript, String.prototype.trim() removes it and /\s/ matches it (both tested in this session with Node). Python's re \s also matches it. A transliterator that trims input or splits on \s will silently destroy Ogham word spaces.

marks.form: A '>' chevron of two straight strokes. They start at full height above and full depth below at the left edge (x 0), and converge to the right on the line at about x 230-294. From that point the stemline begins and runs right (to x 489). It reads like the fletching of an arrow at the start of the line.
marks.note: Opens a text. General category Ps (opening punctuation), checked in this session.

marks.form: The mirror image: the stemline comes in from the left and ends at the point of a '<' chevron, whose two arms open to the right (to x 455).
marks.note: Closes a text. General category Pe (closing punctuation), checked in this session.

lettersSource: The 20 feda in the stone and manuscript order (B L F S N / H D T C Q / M G NG Z R / A O U E I), the five forfeda (EA OI UI IA AE) and peith (P). Names are given in Old Irish forms as in McManus (1991), remembered. Values are given for stones and for manuscripts. Characters, code points and Unicode names come from the Ogham block U+1680-U+169F, checked in this session against UCD 14.0. FORMS are measured stroke by stroke from the glyph outlines of Noto Sans Ogham 2.001 (@fontsource/noto-sans-ogham 5.3.0), outlines measured in this session and re-measured independently in the fact-check (fontTools; every glyph U+1680-169C), horizontal manuscript layout. The page should SET Ogham in this font (ogham subset U+1680-169C; woff2 3,896 bytes, woff 1,960 bytes; SIL OFL 1.1), not draw it. The forms let an illustrator check or reproduce the font and draw a stone-style vertical version. Stone convention: the arris (edge) of the stone is the stemline, read upward (usually up the left edge, sometimes over the top and down). B-group strokes go on one face (to the right), H-group on the other (to the left), M-group across the edge obliquely, vowels as notches on the edge. Medieval manuscript forms of the forfeda vary, and were not compared with the font in this session. Numeric is null: ogham letters carry no numerical values in the tradition. Geometry measured from Noto Sans Ogham 2.001 (@fontsource/noto-sans-ogham 5.3.0), outlines measured in this session, 1000 units/em, horizontal (manuscript) layout read left to right: the stemline is a straight horizontal bar 33 units thick (y 281-314). Each stroke is a straight bar 73 units thick. Strokes of the first two groups are 381 units long. Strokes of a letter are evenly spaced at a pitch of 144 units. The first stroke starts 114 units after the start of the line, and the line runs on 148 units past the last stroke. Glyphs overlap their neighbours by 34 units, so the stemline runs unbroken through a word. All outlines are straight segments: no curves, no ring-ends. Fact-check: font file sizes (woff2 3,896 bytes; woff 1,960 bytes), version 2.001 and licence (OFL-1.1 in the package.json of @fontsource/noto-sans-ogham 5.3.0) confirmed from the local package. Letter names and meanings 'as in McManus (1991), remembered' were not checked.

treeLayers.layer: 1. Original letter names (Primitive Irish, c. 4th-6th c.)
treeLayers.what: A mix of tree names (birch, alder, willow, oak, hazel; perhaps pine and ash) and ordinary words (fear, ingot, field, sulphur, earth...). Meanings are partly uncertain.

treeLayers.layer: 2. Medieval learned doctrine (Auraicept, In Lebor Ogaim; texts of c. 7th-14th c.)
treeLayers.what: Every letter is explained as a tree, sometimes by forced glosses (úath = whitethorn, tinne = holly, gort = ivy). Ogham is "climbed as a tree is climbed". Trees are graded in classes, as in Old Irish law.
treeLayers.source: Calder 1917; Kelly 1976 on the legal tree-list

treeLayers.what: Beth-Luis-Nion order, a 13-month tree calendar with fixed dates, a goddess-cult reading, and divination and "tree astrology". These are not found in any medieval source.

transliterator.notes: Match "ng" before "n". Forfeda digraphs should be an option, off by default, because the stones do not use them. Show modern equivalences for j, y, w, v, k, x and p as conventions, not historical spellings. Never trim() or split on \s (it eats U+1680). For a stone-style display, rotate the horizontal line 90 degrees anticlockwise so that it reads bottom to top.

links.relation: Ogham was built on Latin grammatical analysis, and the Welsh stones pair it with Latin capitals.
Lucian's Ogmios (Heracles 1) in the debate over the name. Macalister's abandoned theory of a Greek-alphabet origin.
Both are northern epigraphic scripts with learned medieval name-poems (rune poems / Bríatharogam). A runic origin for ogham is a minority view.
Cipher comparison: Carney's cipher thesis and the Ogam Tract's substitution oghams against Trithemius's polygraphy.
Same encoding principle: a letter named by group and position in a grid (aicme x number of strokes).
The Auraicept sets Irish and ogham in a Babel frame beside Hebrew, Greek and Latin.
Contrast: ogham is absent from De occulta philosophia (checked in the 1651 English text); it belongs to the wing as a learned, cryptic script with its own tradition.

cautions: FACT-CHECK (2026-10-20): eight web searches ran before the shared search budget ran out. Confirmed: the corpus counts (as sourced in firstAttestation), the 4th-century origin estimate, Ogham in 3D / OG(H)AM, Castell Dwyran's name forms and the dispute over its identification, the Auraicept's dating as given by Wikipedia, Ahlqvist's edition, and the Ogham in 3D URL. Re-checked mechanically: the Unicode data, the whitespace behaviour, every glyph outline, and Agrippa's 1651 text. Everything still marked 'not verified' is the researcher's memory and must be checked before publication.
Keep the three layers apart on the page: original names, medieval tree doctrine, and Graves's modern calendar (treeLayers).
Do not print the Graves tree-calendar dates as tradition. If shown, label them "Graves 1948 / modern".
Do not print a Book of Ballymote folio or a Calder page until checked (ISOS digitisation; Calder 1917). None is given here.
Bríatharogam wordings and their paraphrases are from memory. Check each against Calder 1917 and McManus 1988 before printing.
The bird- and colour-ogham lists are partial and from memory.
The forfeda forms are measured from Noto Sans Ogham. Manuscripts draw the forfeda differently, so do not caption the font forms as "the Book of Ballymote forms".
U+1680 OGHAM SPACE MARK is whitespace (Zs): JavaScript trim() strips it and \s matches it (tested). The transliterator and any validator must allow for this.
Unicode letter names use Modern Irish spellings (BEITH, NION, CEIRT, NGEADAL, EADHADH...); the page text should use Old Irish names and give Unicode names only as labels.
Ogham is not in Agrippa (checked in the 1651 English text, EEBO-TCP A26565). Do not present it as one of his alphabets.
Do not reproduce the emblems or texts of living Druid or Pagan organisations that use ogham.
Mount Callan and other antiquarian "finds" are cautionary tales about forged ogham. Never present an inscription without its corpus number.
Castell Dwyran: do not caption the stone as Vortiporius's (Gildas's tyrant). The identification is disputed (Sims-Williams against Rhŷs), so give it as a proposal.
The vowel lozenges are the font's stylisation. For a stone-style drawing use notches on the arris; for a manuscript-style one, short strokes across the line.
Auraicept dating: give 'core perhaps early 8th century, ascribed by tradition to Cenn Fáelad (d. 679)'. Do not attribute a 7th-century date to Ahlqvist unless his book is checked.
